gotcha_text: Landlords use vague relocation language to force restaurant tenants into inferior, low-traffic units without providing adequate compensation. This allows the landlord to optimize the building's layout for larger anchors while leaving your business to wither in a dead zone.
fix_text: Tenant Pulse identifies ambiguous relocation triggers and flags clauses that lack mandatory build-out reimbursement. It provides precise, industry-standard language to ensure any move is economically viable and physically comparable.
deep_dive_html:
For restaurant operators, a relocation clause is not merely a logistical inconvenience; it is a potential existential threat. Predatory leases often grant landlords the unilateral right to relocate a tenant to a different unit within the center, provided the new space is 'comparable.' However, without rigorous definitions, 'comparable' is a subjective term that landlords exploit to move high-performing tenants into dead zones or spaces with inadequate utility infrastructure.

The Infrastructure Trap

The primary danger lies in the technical requirements of restaurant operations. A landlord may move you to a space that lacks the necessary grease trap capacity, ventilation venting, or electrical load to support your existing kitchen. If your lease does not explicitly mandate that the new space must be 'technically compatible' with your existing equipment and permits, you may be forced to fund a massive, unbudgeted capital expenditure just to remain operational.

The Economic Impact of Substandard Relocation

Relocation also threatens your established customer base. A move from a corner unit with high visibility to an interior unit near a service corridor can decimate foot traffic and destroy the 'goodwill' you have built through years of service. Predatory clauses often fail to account for the loss of visibility and the disruption to delivery logistics, effectively subsidizing the landlord's desire to reconfigure the center at your expense.

Essential Protections to Demand

  • Mandatory Reimbursement: The landlord must pay 100% of all costs associated with the relocation, including permits, construction, and equipment installation.
  • Technical Comparability: The new space must meet all existing utility, plumbing, and ventilation specifications.
  • Visibility Standards: The new unit must maintain equivalent frontage, signage visibility, and foot traffic patterns.
  • Termination Rights: If the new space is deemed unsuitable by a qualified engineer, the tenant must have the right to terminate the lease without penalty.
